newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen says not out to destroy rival.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen says not out to destroy rival.

text.p: Cambodia's strongman Hun Sen insists he is not trying to destroy his rival co-premier in the struggling coalition government and said elections will take place next year despite the country's political woes.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, in an interview with foreign journalists at his "Tiger's Lair" country residence near the capital Phnom Penh on Monday night, also said he had shelved opposition to the royal family taking part in politics.

Strained ties between Hun Sen and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh of the royalist FUNCINPEC party have vitually paralysed Cambodia's government and parliament, political analysts and diplomats have said.
This has delayed the passing of key legislation necessary for holding general elections next year and to enable Cambodia to join the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

Tension between the two men, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993, rose after Hun Sen's call in March for the royal family, headed by King Sihanouk, to be barred from politics. Sihanouk is head of state and Ranariddh's father. The constitution says he reigns but does not rule.
Tensions were exacerbated by a deadly March 30 grenade attack on an opposition rally led by FUNCINPEC ally Sam Rainsy.
Then in mid-April ties neared breaking-point when dissident royalists challenged Ranariddh's leadership of FUNCINPEC and got the backing of Hun Sen and his Cambodian People's Party (CPP).

The premiers, in a bid to allay coup fears at home and abroad sparked by the challenge to Ranariddh, pledged to keep the military and police out of politics and agreed last week to end their bitter public war of words.
"I never have any intention to bring down Ranariddh from being the first prime minister...Ranariddh will continue in his position up to the end of the government," Hun Sen said.
Ranariddh, who has expelled some of the dissidents from FUNCINPEC, has accused the second prime minister of orchestrating the split and of trying to destroy the royalists.
Hun Sen said that despite the political problems he was sure parliament would meet soon and elections, which are due by the end of 1998, would be held.
He said the two parties agreed on fundamental aspects of the electoral law and said he hoped a draft law would be sent to the cabinet soon for review before being voted on in parliament.
Sam Rainsy, the nation's main opposition leader, said on Monday a caretaker government should lead Cambodia to the next general election if ties between Ranariddh and Hun Sen deteriorate.
He told reporters Cambodia was headed for disintegration unless political and diplomatic measures were taken immediately.
Hun Sen also said Cambodia's internal problems should not be used as an excuse to bar it from joining ASEAN.
Some political analysts have suggested political strife in Cambodia could delay its entry.
Cambodia, Laos and Burma are due to join the seven-member ASEAN later this year. The group comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
In a move that could ease tension, Hun Sen said he had changed his mind about barring Cambodia's royalty from politics.
He had said in March that either the royal family should agree voluntarily to refrain from politics or a public referendum should be held on the issue.
"I will not support any move to ban the royal family from being involved in politics," Hun Sen said.
